item.title: “Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A…
item.description:
“Fear, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Suffering, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Disease, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A boil, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A dart, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Bondage, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. Mud, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures. A womb, monks, is a synonym for sensual pleasures.
How, monks, is fear a synonym for sensual pleasures? Because those who are infected by sensual desire, bound by sensual lust, are not freed from fear in the present life, not freed from fear in the future — therefore fear is a synonym for sensual pleasures.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.56

item.title: Elder Nun Sundarī Nandā: Nandā, look at this body — Diseased, impure, stinking. Develop the mind on foulness, One-pointed, well-concentrated. As this body, so that…
item.description:
Elder Nun Sundarī Nandā:

Nandā, look at this body —
Diseased, impure, stinking.
Develop the mind on foulness,
One-pointed, well-concentrated.

As this body, so that body —
As that body, so this body —
Foul, rotting —
Only fools delight in it.

Thus contemplate this body,
Day and night without fatigue.
With your own wisdom,
Therefore escape.
With your own wisdom,
Escape pride in beauty,
And see truly
What fools see.

This city is built of bones,
Plastered with flesh and blood.
Within dwell aging and death,
Conceit and hypocrisy.

Without heedlessness,
Rightly contemplate that body —
The true nature of this body
Is seen inside and out.
I am disenchanted with the body,
My mind is dispassionate.
Without heedlessness, free from bonds,
I am at peace, stilled.

From: Therīgāthā 5.4

item.title: “Monks, just as a defiled, dust-covered cloth, when a dyer dips it in this or that dye – blue, yellow, red, or purple – will…
item.description:
“Monks, just as a defiled, dust-covered cloth, when a dyer dips it in this or that dye – blue, yellow, red, or purple – will take the dye poorly and be unclean. Why is that? Because the cloth is not clean. So too, monks, a foul destination awaits a defiled mind. Monks, just as a clean, bright cloth, when a dyer dips it in this or that dye – blue, yellow, red, or purple – will take the dye well and be clean. Why is that? Because the cloth is clean. So too, monks, a good destination awaits an undefiled mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthūpamasutta

item.title: “Monk, whoever thinks about form is bound by Māra. Whoever does not think about form is freed from the Evil One. Whoever thinks about feeling…
item.description:
“Monk, whoever thinks about form is bound by Māra. Whoever does not think about form is freed from the Evil One. Whoever thinks about feeling … perception … formations … consciousness is bound by Māra. Whoever does not think about consciousness is freed from the Evil One. This brief saying of mine, monk, should be understood in detail.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.64

item.title: “Monks, I will teach you nine things rooted in craving. Listen and pay close attention. And what, monks, are the nine things rooted in craving?…
item.description:
“Monks, I will teach you nine things rooted in craving. Listen and pay close attention. And what, monks, are the nine things rooted in craving? Dependent on craving, seeking arises; dependent on seeking, gain arises; dependent on gain, decision arises; dependent on decision, desire and lust arise; dependent on desire and lust, attachment arises; dependent on attachment, possessiveness arises; dependent on possessiveness, guarding arises; dependent on guarding, the taking up of sticks and swords, quarrels, disputes, arguments, slander, false speech, and many evil, unwholesome states arise. These, monks, are the nine things rooted in craving.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.23

item.title: “Monks, if a monk, reflecting thus, knows: ‘I dwell much with a greedy mind; I dwell much with a hateful mind; I dwell much with…
item.description:
“Monks, if a monk, reflecting thus, knows: ‘I dwell much with a greedy mind; I dwell much with a hateful mind; I dwell much with a mind overcome by sloth and torpor; I dwell much with restlessness; I dwell much with doubt; I dwell much with anger; I dwell much with a defiled mind; I dwell much with bodily fever; I dwell much with laziness; I dwell much unconcentrated’ — then that monk should make a strong wish, arouse effort, be energetic, strive, be strong-minded, not fall away, be mindful and clearly comprehending for the abandonment of those evil, unwholesome states. Just as, monks, if a turban or head were on fire, one would make a strong wish, arouse effort, be energetic, strive, be strong-minded, not fall away, be mindful and clearly comprehending to extinguish that turban or head — so too, that monk should make a strong wish … for the abandonment of those evil, unwholesome states.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.51

item.title: “And how, monks, is there non-restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is attached to agreeable forms and repelled…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is there non-restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is attached to agreeable forms and repelled by disagreeable forms. He dwells with bodily mindfulness unestablished, with a limited mind. He does not know as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are not abandoned without remainder. Thus, monks, is non-restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.244

item.title: “And what, Ānanda, is the path, the way leading to the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a monk, by the relinquishment of…
item.description:
“And what, Ānanda, is the path, the way leading to the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a monk, by the relinquishment of attachments (upadhiviveka), by the abandoning of unwholesome states, by the complete calming of bodily coarseness, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 64 – Mahāmāluṅkyasutta

item.title: (Calā): Having been born, one must die, Seeing suffering in birth, Fetters and afflictions — Therefore I do not delight in birth. The Buddha has…
item.description:
(Calā):
Having been born, one must die,
Seeing suffering in birth,
Fetters and afflictions —
Therefore I do not delight in birth.
The Buddha has taught the Dhamma
That leads beyond renewed existence,
Abolishing all suffering —
He has established me in truth.
Beings headed for the form realm,
Those aspiring to the formless realm,
If they do not know cessation,
They go to renewed existence.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.6

item.title: “Householder, just as a house with a badly thatched roof — the ridgepole is not protected, the rafters are not protected, the walls are not…
item.description:
“Householder, just as a house with a badly thatched roof — the ridgepole is not protected, the rafters are not protected, the walls are not protected; the ridgepole becomes soaked and leaks, the rafters become soaked and leak, the walls become soaked and leak; the ridgepole rots, the rafters rot, the walls rot. So too, householder, when the mind is not guarded, bodily actions are not guarded, verbal actions … mental actions … then bodily actions become soaked with greed and leak, verbal actions become soaked with greed and leak, mental actions become soaked with greed and leak. For one whose bodily actions are soaked and leak with greed, whose verbal and mental actions are soaked and leak with greed, bodily actions rot, verbal actions rot, mental actions rot. For one whose bodily, verbal, and mental actions rot, death is not good, the end is not good.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.109
